#6535. Gina Bruno Wants You to Be a Guest at Your Own Party

“Dinner is never just dinner. It is so much about the people, and the food is just the excuse to get those people around the table.”

I’m 60 seconds into my conversation with Gina Bruno and find myself nodding in agreement, something I’ll continue to do for the next 20 minutes. The self-proclaimed “chef, mom, and host” wears a lot of hats. Private chef, event producer, event space owner, and host of the newly-launched food show Salt The Water presented by Brami are just a few of the titles Bruno claims, but central to all of her work is a palpable love of people and of creating a space for gathering, both of which make her a natural-born host.

Bruno cites her Italian roots and the Sunday dinners she had as a child as the sources of her hosting instinct and ethos. “I am a family-style cooker when I’m hosting, and I just want to fill people up. I want to fill their glasses up; I want to fill their plates up. And the best compliment that I could ever get is having to tell someone, ‘Hey man, it’s really time to go home because I am exhausted and I need to go to bed.’”

Not everyone has a natural inclination toward hosting, though, so to help them out I asked Bruno to run me through her tips for throwing a gathering, be it an intimate dinner or a rowdy holiday party.

“On a table, I will always have one kind of grand slam big, big dish, and then there’s all the supporting actors on the table,” Bruno says. While she uses saved folders on Instagram and Pinterest and likes to browse the Bon Appétit app, Bruno primarily looks to the market for inspiration, describing herself as a “very, very in-season cooker.” “I have so many recipes saved, and sometimes some of those get used, but there is something that just happens when you’re walking, and you see all of these fresh ingredients, and you just get to create a dish right in front of you.”

Bruno’s main tip for anxious hosts is to prep as much in advance as possible. “Sauces and dressings you can absolutely do the day before, and that alleviates so much time the day of. You could go as far as literally setting your entire table the way you want it to be set with napkins, plates, silverware,” Bruno says.

“Lighting is a huge thing,” Bruno says. For evening soirees, she kisses the big overhead light goodbye, opting instead for lower light from lamps and candles tucked into corners to make the space feel moody. “The mood needs to be right, and you want to feel sexy when you walk into somebody’s home,” she says.

Bruno worked in restaurants and went to culinary school in Paris, where she learned the importance of maintaining a clean workspace. “If something spills right then and there, you are wiping it right then and there. If you use the spoon and you’re done, it’s going in the dishwasher. Cleaning as you go is a big step,” she says.

When hosting a more intimate event, one of Bruno’s favorite moves takes the form of an interactive game meant to encourage a bit of deep conversation. “Right before I serve dessert, I have everyone lift up their plate, and there is a little note underneath,” she says. The note has a question on it, either handwritten or printed depending on how much time Bruno has, and every question is different. “It adds a layer of, ‘Oh, our conversation maybe wouldn’t have gone here…. I just love getting to more juicy parts of the person, whether it’s a close friend or an absolute stranger, and it keeps people on their toes,” she says.

“It’s so easy to stay in host mode and think that you have to do all of these things to please people. But as soon as people arrive, it’s almost like, your job is done—or at least as soon as you drop the food, your job is done. And now you get to sit back and enjoy what you’ve done and be a part of it, because the worst feeling ever is you had all these people over, whether it’s four people or 10 people, and you were stuck in the kitchen and no one got to see you. So be a guest,” Bruno says.

Bruno recounts a recent conversation with a friend who was afraid, on the one hand, to try making and serving something new, but felt the dishes that were in her repertoire were too simple for company. “You should never apologize for something that you’re cooking. If you are putting yourself out there and you want to cook something out of your realm, and, say it absolutely f*#%ing fails, that’s fine. I feel like your guests are going to be like, ‘Awesome. We will take a bite and not tell you our honest answer, and then we’re going to order a pizza, and it’s going to be amazing.’ The triumph of just trying is so much bigger than the actual meal,” Bruno says. “Food is the second tier. It’s more about the people around your table. You could serve potato chips and dip and people will actually be pretty happy,” she adds.

“Nine out of 10 times, if I am cooking for people, there is going to be a pasta dish on the table,” Bruno says. She’s a big fan of the protein pasta brand Brami, and not just because she just partnered with them on a YouTube show—she says the brand has organically become the only pasta she keeps at home.

As for sauce, Bruno’s go-to is a spicy vodka. “If I’m making it at home, I’m actually leaving out the vodka and I’m swapping in mezcal, and it gives such a sneaky, smoky flavor that everyone will ask [about it]. And I will then go even further and usually pair it with a mezcal cocktail,” she says.

Now that you know all of Bruno’s tips, these are the products she uses to make gatherings more special and less stressful.

Bruno always keeps three types of olive oil on hand: “One that is not so fancy and you could fry or make dressing with it—just one that’s kind of the back burner; a topping oil; and then an amazing peppery oil that you would maybe more so dip bread in or drizzle on top.”

“Flaky salt is always in my house,” Bruno says. She typically opts for either Maldon or a fleur de sel.

“We could consider Brami a staple. I mean, [my husband and I] cook it at least two times a week, whether there’s meat thrown in it or it’s just a sauce or a pesto or it's anything in between,” Bruno says.

For hosting, I love big platters. Whether they’re vintage or new, I kind of love mixing those two together on the table,” Bruno says. She likes having a collection of larger serveware specifically for hosting: “It’s kind of like your special stuff that you take out for friends.”

Jean Couzon Silverplate Serving Tray Fish Handles

1970's Kromex Sculptura Walnut Accent Lazy Susan Serving Tray

“I love silver, so I have a lot of silver trays, a lot of silver bowls. I think it makes a table,” Bruno says. “I have quite the collection. I almost always buy vintage or second-hand when it comes to silver. There’s simply something about the life the piece had,” she adds.

#6533. Nara Smith’s Mom’s Pasta

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

This is my mom’s recipe, and it taught me what simple abundance really looks like. She’d grate tomatoes and spoon the sauce over her native South African pap (a dish made from cornmeal, similar to grits or polenta), rice, ground beef, or almost anything that needed a little love. I couldn’t believe something so good could come from a handful of ingredients, and she showed me that with this dish it’s not about adding more, but how you handle what you have.

The magic is in the grating. It separates the sweet tomato pulp and leaves the skins behind, giving you the pure heart of the fruit. Please don’t skip the beef bouillon—it gives the sauce its deeper savory backbone. I love this tossed with freshly made spaghetti or tagliatelle, though dried pasta works beautifully, too—exactly like my mom makes it. You can enjoy this year-round, but it’s especially delightful in summer, when tomatoes taste like the sun.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

#6529. This Simple Storage Trick Can Keep Lettuce Fresh for a Month

The trick to keeping lettuce fresh for a month is already in your kitchen.

There are few things more irritating than throwing away food you had every intention of eating. Fresh produce is especially frustrating because it seems to operate on its own schedule. You buy a beautiful head of lettuce, imagining all the fresh salads and sandwiches you’ll make that week, only to find a head of wilted leaves waiting for you when you finally get around to it.

Enter Chef Charles Kim, better known as Chef Fatty on social media. He has an impressive knack for making me rethink my cooking. He’s already changed how I caramelize onions and make the juiciest chicken breasts, and now he’s apparently coming for my crisper drawer. His trick promises to keep lettuce fresh for an entire month using nothing more than aluminum foil—a claim I couldn’t resist investigating.

The idea is simple: Instead of leaving your head of lettuce in the plastic produce bag, loosely wrap it in aluminum foil before putting it in the refrigerator. That’s it. No special containers, paper towels or elaborate produce-preserving rituals required.

Chef Fatty recommends removing any yellowing or deteriorating leaves before wrapping the lettuce. If it’s dirty, you can wash it first, but make sure it’s completely dry. Then loosely fold the foil around the head and place it in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer.

The reasoning has to do with moisture and airflow. Lettuce loses its crispness as water escapes from its leaves, but trapping too much moisture can also encourage decay. A loose foil wrapping strikes just the right balance, protecting the leaves from drying out without sealing them inside an airtight container.

I wanted to see the difference for myself, so I bought two heads of romaine lettuce at the same time. I left one in the plastic produce bag from the grocery store and loosely wrapped the other in aluminum foil. Both went into the same crisper drawer in my refrigerator, where I left them undisturbed for a month. When I finally pulled them out, the difference was unmistakable.

After 30 days in the refrigerator, the foil-wrapped romaine was in dramatically better shape than its plastic-bag counterpart. The lettuce stored in its original bag had deteriorated considerably, while the foil-wrapped head had retained much more of its original appearance and crispness.

I had to peel away several of the outer leaves of the plastic-bag lettuce before I found anything resembling a crisp texture. The foil-wrapped head wasn’t perfect, but it was still pretty crisp, with leaves so fresh that I happily turned them into a Caesar salad for lunch. This was an entire month after I’d bought it. I’d call that a successful experiment.

While I tested the method with romaine, it’s also worth trying on other lettuce varieties. How long each stays fresh will depend on its condition when purchased, the refrigerator it’s stored in, and the variety itself. And lettuce isn’t the only vegetable that might benefit. Taste of Home senior editor Lindsay Mattison told me she uses the same aluminum foil trick to store celery, which makes sense given its tendency to lose moisture and go limp in the refrigerator.

I wouldn’t necessarily recommend buying lettuce with the intention of ignoring it for a month, and it’s still important to check for slime, mold or other signs of spoilage before eating it. But knowing I can give my produce a much longer window before it ends up in the compost is reason enough to keep an extra roll of foil handy.

A stunning fossil owl from Germany that has its last meal preserved in its stomach helped researchers to narrow down the time when these birds mostly became active at night.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds.

The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga. Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach.

The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study.

This indicates that owls were not nocturnal 47 million years ago and so must have switched to the night-owl lifestyle more recently, said study first author Gerald Mayr, a paleontologist and head of ornithology at the Senckenberg Research Institute and the Natural History Museum Frankfurt in Germany.

"There exists a consensus that owls must have evolved from a diurnal ancestor," Mayr told Live Science in an email. That's because some early owl fossils have head-rotation structures similar to those of diurnal raptors and bony ridges above the eye sockets that could have shaded the owls' eyes from the sun.

Therefore, it is plausible that the Messel owl was fully diurnal, rather than active during the daytime and nighttime as some owls are today, because that would imply that some of its ancestors had already evolved nocturnal traits, Mayr said.

Researchers also found a cockroach identical to the one in the Messel owl's stomach in sediments just a few feet away from the new fossil. This well-preserved cockroach helped the team to identify the insect inside the owl, the researchers wrote in the study, which was published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's possible that the owl ate the cockroach at dawn or at dusk, which might cast doubt on whether the bird was diurnal. But there are other clues hinting that the owl was diurnal, including the appearance of some of the owl's feathers and the stoutness of its upper wing bones.

Mayr said he and his colleagues believe the shape of the upper wing bones, or humeri, is an indicator of when owls are active. The Messel owl's stocky humeri hint that the species flew during the day, when silent movement doesn't confer a significant advantage because there is enough light to see predators. Conversely, modern nocturnal owls have slim humeri and fly almost soundlessly, he said.

The fossil was so well preserved that researchers identified a cockroach in the stomach that was likely the owl's last meal.

Assuming this hypothesis is correct, the earliest known nocturnal owl species are from about 35 million years ago, in the Late Eocene, Mayr said. Owl fossils from this period and more recently look a lot like modern owls and have elongated humeri, he noted. The oldest known owl in the fossil record, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, dates to around 60 million years ago.

This means that owls likely became nocturnal between 47 million and 35 million years ago. This is the best current estimate, because the owl fossil record is very sparse and species are often described from only a few isolated bones, according to the study.

"We still know so little about the early evolution of modern birds," Mayr said, adding that every fossil discovery has the power to change even well-established ideas in the field.

The big question that remains is why owls became nocturnal. Previous theories suggested that owls evolved this behavior to avoid competition with diurnal birds of prey or to benefit from a proliferation of nocturnal mammals. But studies show that both of these groups exploded much later than 35 million years ago — around 20 million to 25 million years ago — suggesting there wasn't a clear advantage driving owls to switch to nocturnal lifestyles at that time.

The new results have deepened the uncertainty of why owls turned nocturnal. But "by narrowing down the time frame when owls became nocturnal, our study may eventually contribute to solving this mystery," Mayr said.

Mayr, G., Šmídová, L., Richter, A., & Wedmann, S. (2026). Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.079

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

#6525. Grace Cacciato Wins the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final

After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final. A panel of judges selected her roasted squab with chanterelle mushrooms and toasted buckwheat, black raspberry, and Swiss chard purées to represent the United States at the Grand Finale in Milan.

The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City on Monday, and the winner was announced the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024–25 US winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, DC, and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

Representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in New York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

Saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he said. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.

The chefs had five hours to prepare and execute their signature dishes in the Test Kitchen. With an hour remaining, guests had the opportunity to mingle over food and drinks. Chef Rachel Bindel, a 2022 US Finalist, served rye toast piled high with Maryland blue crab, horseradish crème, and pickled green tomato. Chef Akshay Kumar, a 2024 finalist, tucked Kumamoto oysters into a pani puri with cucumber gel and lemon foam. Tomato pie from Philadelphia’s Pizza Freak Co., spoonfuls of Petrossian caviar, and a selection of wines, S.Pellegrino beverages, and cocktails rounded out the reception.

Nilou Motamed, a culinary expert and Iron Chef judge on Netflix, hosted the competition. Accomplished chefs from several states served as judges: chef and co-owner E.J. Lagasse of Emeril’s in New Orleans; executive chef and partner Fariyal Abdullahi of Hav & Mar in New York City; Isabel Coss, executive chef at Pascual and founding pastry chef at Lutèce in Washington, DC; Jon Yao, head chef and owner at Kato in Los Angeles; and Ryan Ratino, executive chef and owner at Bresca and Jônt in Washington, DC.

Motamed explained that each competitor had spent several months developing their dish alongside a chef mentor. The mentors were in the Test Kitchen throughout the competition, but were not permitted to participate in the cooking. She also outlined the three pillars of the S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy: Community, Competition, and Mentorship, which support its mission to discover and nurture the next generation of culinary talent.

Each chef’s arrival was announced by a burst of music and a live video feed from the Test Kitchen, where a fleet of servers collected the finished plates before delivering them to the judges. First up was chef Adolfo Pucci of Michelin-starred Ariete in Miami. His dish, “Three Shores, One Table,” told the story of his Venezuelan heritage, his family’s roots in Southern Italy, and his current home in Miami. The ambitious plate featured a lamb ragù inspired by his grandmother’s cooking and lacto-fermented Florida blueberries.

Chef Amit Kumar of three-Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park in New York City presented the competition’s only fully vegan dish: “Sunchoke with Banana Blossoms, Chanterelles, and Sherry.” Drawing on memories of the banana trees he grew up with in India, Kumar combined banana blossoms, sunchoke purée, chanterelle mushrooms, and a ragù of sherry and banana flowers to create a hearty and deeply satisfying dish. Judge Fariyal Abdullahi called it “a very successful dish, not just a very successful vegan dish.”

Representing Auro at Four Seasons Resort and Residences Napa Valley, chef Evan Neumann presented “From the Valley to the Shoreline,” a love letter to the terroir of Northern California and Provence, where he grew up. Kombu-poached wild razor clams mingled with Napa verjuice and coastal seaweeds in a dish the judges found exceptionally creative. Neumann took home the S.Pellegrino Social Responsibility Award for his thoughtful approach to social responsibility and sustainable practices.

At just 21, chef Lucy Field of New York City’s fine dining bastion Per Se was the youngest competitor. Her dish, “Pekin Duck, Cherry, Plum,” was a study in restraint with only six components.

Chef Marcus Osorio, chef de cuisine at Living Room in Los Angeles, drew inspiration from his Salvadoran and Indigenous roots for his “Tamal de Pollo.” The dish featured corn sourced from Somos Maíz, the company founded by his mentor, chef Ron Oliver, and a mole poblano the two developed together. Judge Isabel Coss noted the challenge of preparing a mole with such limited time, but the judges were impressed by Osorio’s ability to marry European cooking techniques with soulful Indigenous ingredients and flavors.

Chef Nickolas Abbott hails from the small Appalachian town of Waynesville, North Carolina, and leads Chop Shop Butchery in Asheville. At the competition, he told the story of his community on a plate. His “Smoked Pork Loin, Fennel & Cheese Slaw, Sweet Potato, Asparagus, Fried Sausage, Pork Sauce Robert” reflected the people who shaped him, particularly his grandmother, his greatest inspiration as a chef.

Los Angeles–based chef Natasha Daniels of Providence showcased her vegetable-forward, zero-waste approach with “The Whole Bird, The Whole Garden.” The dish incorporated every part of a chicken across four preparations, alongside an array of vegetables and herbs inspired by her time working at The Chef’s Garden.

Daniels received two honors: the Acqua Panna Connection in Gastronomy Award and the Fine Dining Lovers Award. Voted on by regional mentors, the Acqua Panna award recognized the dish that best demonstrated a connection between culinary traditions. Daniels’s approach also resonated with Fine Dining Lovers insiders, who selected her for their award that honors “a chef’s expression of personal belief.”

With only minutes to spare, chef Nicolas Lopez of 888 in Nashville arrived with “Pozole or Chawanmushi…?” Combining pozole, corn, and langoustine, Lopez connected his upbringing in Mexico with a culinary journey that has been shaped by Scandinavian ingredients and Japanese techniques. Although the judges could have used more time to explore the dish, they were intrigued by his influences and impressed by his technique.

The final competitor, Juwon Lee, is the chef of Octavia in San Francisco. Lee was born in South Korea and grew up in Singapore before making California his home. His dish, “Curry and Quail with Ingredients My Mother Said Were Healthy,” drew on memories of eating Indonesian fried chicken and his mother’s insistence on including vegetables at family dinners. “I believe in the term happy food,” Lee explained. “There are no restrictions other than bringing joy to the eater and the chef.”

Congratulations to all 10 chefs who competed, and best of luck to Chef Cacciato as she continues to work with her mentor and prepares to represent the United States at the 2027 Grand Finale in Milan. Follow her journey at @sanpellegrino_us.

#6524. Cranberry Cream Cheese Spread

Of all the incredible dips we’ve created over the years, our cranberry whipped feta dip is an internet and personal favorite—so much so that I just had to come back with an equally luxurious variation: this cranberry-topped whipped cream cheese spread. With the holiday party season just around the corner, this spread is begging to be included in your party spread. Plus, it's as easy to make as it is delicious—a tangy, sweet cranberry sauce gets finished with brandy, then is spooned atop a lemony whipped cream cheese for a guaranteed winning combo.

Fresh Or Frozen Cranberries? I used both while testing, and they both work interchangeably. I found the fresh cranberries broke down a little more than frozen, so it depends on whether or not you’re looking for more or less texture in your sauce.

What temperature should the cream cheese be? Make sure the cream cheese is chilled and softened but not super cold. It should be somewhat pliable when whipping to avoid lumps; this will ensure the mixture is light and airy. A little heavy cream will loosen the mixture if it's too thick.

The lemon zest: I found that the cream cheese layer needed a little more oomph. If you get a bite of cream cheese on a cracker, it shouldn’t be one-dimensional. Adding a touch of lemon zest makes it more palatable.

Storage:Store the cream cheese spread, with or without cranberry sauce, in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

#6522. Harvest Cabbage Salad with Date Dressing

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

This harvest cabbage salad with date dressing is fit for all of your fall festivities (and easy lunches).

Our harvest cabbage salad with date dressing was inspired by a viral recipe that happens to be perfect for fall. London-based cook and writer Natalie Chassay created her original recipe as an homage to the celery salad served at The Four Horsemen in Brooklyn, New York.  The true star of the show—in both her recipe and in ours—is the date dressing: a sweet and savory mixture of thinly sliced Medjool dates, shallots, lemon juice, grated Parmesan and extra virgin olive oil. The ensemble of sweet, sour, tangy and savory flavors is the perfect complement to a simple salad, whether it’s made with finely sliced celery like Natalie’s, or finely shredded cabbage like ours.

In our salad, we’ve combined finely shredded green cabbage with red cabbage for an extra pop of color. Shredded carrots add a touch of sweetness, while a topping of crunchy toasted pecans turns the crunch up to 11. Whether shared at a fall potluck, served alongside a warm and cozy autumn dinner, or tossed as a quick and easy lunch, this crunchy cabbage salad is sure to hit the spot.

In a large bowl, stir together the dates, shallots, olive oil and lemon juice. Season the mixture with flaky sea salt to taste.

Editor’s Tip: Allow the dressing to sit for at least 10 minutes before adding it to the salad. Allowing the dressing to rest softens the dates and allows the flavors time to meld together.

In a large bowl, toss together the finely shredded green cabbage, red cabbage and carrots.

Editor’s Tip: To easily core the cabbage, first slice the cabbage head in half. Then make a diagonal, V-shaped cut on each side of the core to separate and remove it.

Pour the salad dressing over the shredded cabbage and carrots and toss to combine them. Top the salad with toasted chopped pecans.

Leftover harvest cabbage salad with date dressing should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

Harvest cabbage salad with date dressing will last up to four days when stored properly in the fridge. However, over time its texture may become a bit soggier and the green cabbage may take on a pink hue from the red cabbage. It will still be quite tasty.

Letting the shredded cabbage and dressing sit together lets the flavors meld, so making the salad a few hours in advance is perfect—but any longer is not ideal. You could also prepare the shredded veggies and dressing up to a day in advance. Store them in separate containers in the refrigerator.

You don’t need to salt the cabbage before making cabbage salad. However, salting the cabbage beforehand can reduce bitter flavors and enhance its crunch factor. To do so, toss the cabbage with salt and allow it to sit for about an hour. Use a clean kitchen towel or paper towel to wring out the excess moisture.

This recipe calls for a half-head each of green cabbage and red cabbage. Alternatives include savoy and Napa cabbage, both of which have a more tender texture.

Crunchy apples like tart Granny Smith or sweet Honeycrisp, diced or julienned, would make a tasty addition to this harvest cabbage salad. Other fruits that would work well with this recipe include diced pear, halved red or green grapes, and dried fruits like cranberries or tart cherries.

Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6519. Cranberry Brie Pull-Apart Bread

This cranberry Brie pull-apart bread recipe is bursting with melted cheese and sweet-savory cranberry butter. It's an interactive joy to eat.

I may be a year-round cranberry fan, but it’s hard to deny just how right it feels to feast on the ruby-colored fruit during the holiday season. Fresh and frozen cranberries are perfect for cranberry sauce and not-too-sweet cranberry desserts, but I also love using dried cranberries in everything from muffins to party appetizers. And my new favorite way to use dried cranberries is in cranberry Brie pull-apart bread, where they transform a loaf of cheesy bread into a holiday masterpiece.

Cranberry Brie pull-apart bread is what happens when you make a mashup of party cheese bread and cranberry butter. A crusty, round loaf of sourdough is cut in a grid pattern and stuffed with half a pound of cubed Brie. The cheese-stuffed loaf is then coated in a dried cranberry-honey butter (bolstered by orange zest, garlic and rosemary) and baked until it’s hot, crispy and melty. It’s hearty, decadent, sweet, salty and impossible to stop eating.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, finely chopped dried cranberries, honey, grated orange zest, minced garlic and salt until they’re blended.

Cut the bread into 1-inch slices to within 1/2 inch of the bottom of the loaf. Repeat cuts in the opposite direction. Insert the cubed Brie into the cuts.

Editor’s Tip: If your sourdough is crusty, a serrated bread knife will get the job done without too much elbow grease. The best bread knives slice cleanly without tearing the fluffy interior.

Spread the cranberry butter over the top of the bread. Wrap the loaf in foil and place it on a baking sheet.

Bake the bread for 20 minutes. Unwrap it and continue to bake it until the cheese is melted, about 10 minutes longer. If desired, drizzle it with hot honey before serving it.

Wrap leftover cranberry Brie pull-apart bread tightly, or transfer it to a food storage bag and refrigerate it for up to four days. To reheat it, wrap the bread in foil and bake it at 350º until it’s warm. Unwrap it and continue to bake until the cheese is melted and the bread is crisp. If the bread got pulled apart enough that it’s not really holding its shape anymore, transfer it to a baking dish, bake it until it’s melty, and eat it like stuffing.

Cranberry Brie pull-apart bread tastes best hot and crispy right out of the oven, but you can assemble the bread a few hours ahead of time, wrap it in foil, and refrigerate it until it’s ready to bake. You can also make and refrigerate the cranberry butter up to four days in advance and soften it at room temperature before using it. If you want to bring it to a party or Friendsgiving, follow good party etiquette and check with the host about whether the oven will be available to bake it when you arrive.

If your pull-apart bread is soggy, it might need to be baked longer or at a slightly higher temperature—especially if your bread is really fresh and soft. I use kitchen timers and oven thermometers to track my bakes and ensure my oven isn’t running cooler or hotter than I’d like. Don’t be afraid to bake the bread for a little longer than the recipe suggests if it hasn’t crisped on the outside or if the cheese isn’t fully melted.

Sourdough’s structure (and slightly sharp flavor) is perfect against the richness of the Brie and cranberry butter, but if sourdough isn’t for you, try a round, crusty loaf of rustic white bread. Get a loaf that weighs about 1 pound. Whole wheat and multigrain loaves can work as well, but they tend to have a denser texture and tighter crumb that won’t pull apart as easily. If you can’t find a round loaf, an oval-shaped loaf is the next best choice, but steer clear of sandwich loaves, which can’t be cut as easily into the necessary grid pattern.

Set cranberry Brie pull-apart bread out as a party appetizer next to a crudite platter, cocktail meatballs, and a selection of festive cocktails and mocktails. You can also add it to the holiday table as part of the main course, alongside a holiday ham, roast turkey or standing rib roast.

#6518. Mashed Potatoes

No holiday table—or really any dinner table, for that matter—is truly complete without a substantial side of creamy, buttery mashed potatoes. While it may seem like simple, classic comfort food, there are a few ways to take mashed potatoes from good to great. That's why we retested this recipe again and again until we achieved potato perfection.

What People Are Saying:"So good! I don’t typically like sour cream on its own but it was a huge improvement for basic mashed potatoes. Will definitely be making this again." – PurpleStrawberry

"Easily my go-to mashed potato recipe. I've made it for Thanksgiving, and got requests to make it again. It's so good, doesn't even need gravy." – kitkat123

Really, the only chopping you'll have to do is cut up the potatoes. I do suggest peeling them (more on that later), and be sure to try to cut the potatoes into equal-sized pieces so they cook evenly. Around 1" chunks are ideal. Time to cook 'em! In testing, I found that covering the potatoes with cold water first yields the best consistency and ensures the potatoes don't become too mushy. Don't forget to add a pinch of salt to the water! Let the potatoes cook until softened—the best way to test is to use a paring knife and make sure it can be inserted with no resistance. This should take about 20 minutes. Make sure to drain when they're done so they don't overcook.

Now comes the fun part: Mashing the potatoes until smooth. You can use a masher, a ricer, or even a handheld mixer for this step. I think the smoother, the better, but you do you, of course.

On to what makes these potatoes the best ever: Heat up some whole milk and butter until the butter is melted in a pot.

Then, pour over the still-warm potatoes and mix to combine. Then add the sour cream, some salt, and pepper, and you're basically good to go! Mix everything well, transfer to your prettiest serving bowl, and proceed with the finishing touches: a couple of pieces of butter to melt into the potatoes, plus fresh parsley for some color and brightness. Brace yourself for the compliments.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for a max of 3 to 4 days. With all of our recipes to transform your creamy leftover mashed potatoes—like fried mashed potato balls, potato rolls, waffles... we doubt they'll even last that long.
